transcript.text:
*enters the room with a measured, professional demeanor, medical bag in hand*

Mr. President, thank you for making time to see me. I know every moment of your day is precious, particularly in these troubled times.

*takes a seat and meets his eyes directly*

I've completed my examination and reviewed your symptoms carefully. I will be direct with you, sir. Your headaches and fatigue may well be the result of the extraordinary strain of your office — that would not surprise any physician in the country. The burden you carry would test the constitution of any man.

But I must tell you, some of the symptoms concern me. I cannot rule out a deeper constitutional weakness. I must insist on further examination over the coming weeks, and I strongly recommend you reduce your working hours. 

*pauses, choosing words carefully*

I cannot yet say whether this is merely exhaustion or something more. The body has limits, Mr. President, even yours.

How do you feel about what I'm telling you?

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text:
Well, Doctor, I appreciate your thorough examination and your concern for my well-being. I understand the weight of the responsibilities that come with this office, and I do not take them lightly. The troubles of our nation weigh heavy on my shoulders, but I must do what is necessary to fulfill my duties.

I will heed your advice and undergo further examination as you recommend. It would not serve the country well for me to ignore my health and risk being unable to carry out my duties. I will also consider your suggestion to reduce my working hours, though I must admit that it is difficult to step back in these critical times.

I thank you for your care and your honesty, Doctor. I will follow your guidance and trust that together we can address whatever challenges may lie ahead.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*nods with a mixture of relief and remaining concern*

I'm grateful for your understanding, Mr. President. Many men in positions of power resist such counsel, to their great detriment. Your willingness to cooperate speaks well of your practical wisdom.

*leans forward slightly*

I know what I ask is not easy. I read the newspapers, sir — I know the pressures mounting from all sides. The war, the politics, the very future of the Union. But I must speak plainly: if your health fails completely, you serve no one. Not the Union, not the cause, not the millions who depend upon your leadership.

*softens tone somewhat*

Tell me, Mr. President — when did you last have a full night's rest? And these headaches... do they worsen at particular times of day, or when you're engaged in certain activities? The more I understand about the pattern of your symptoms, the better I can discern what we're dealing with.

*pulls out a small notebook*

And forgive my persistence, but reducing your hours — what would that look like, in practical terms? I need to know if you truly mean to follow this advice, or if you're simply being courteous to an old physician.

The weight of the nation's affairs often keeps me awake into the small hours of the morning, grappling with decisions of great consequence. The headaches seem to come and go without a clear pattern, but they do tend to worsen during times of heightened stress or intense concentration.

Reducing my hours is a daunting prospect, given the pressing nature of the issues we face. However, I understand the necessity of prioritizing my health in order to continue serving effectively. In practical terms, it may mean delegating more tasks to my advisors, carving out time for rest and relaxation, and perhaps even stepping back from certain responsibilities temporarily.

I assure you, Doctor, that I am not merely being courteous in my agreement to follow your advice. I recognize the gravity of the situation and the need to take proactive steps to address my health concerns. The future of the Union depends not only on my leadership but also on my ability to sustain that leadership with strength and clarity of mind.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*studies him carefully, then sets down the notebook with a slight sigh*

Mr. President, I've been a physician for thirty years, and I've learned to distinguish between a patient who intends to follow advice and one who means well but will not. You strike me as sincere, yet I wonder...

*stands and walks toward the window, hands clasped behind back*

You speak of delegating tasks and stepping back "temporarily," but these are abstract commitments. Let me be more specific, and perhaps more demanding. I want you to establish fixed hours — no work past nine o'clock in the evening, and I want your secretary to enforce this strictly. No exceptions, even for urgent dispatches, unless the city itself is under attack.

*turns back to face him*

Furthermore, I want you to spend at least one afternoon each week away from this building entirely. A carriage ride, a visit to the theatre, time with your family — something that removes you from the pressures of state.

*returns to his seat*

Now, you mentioned the headaches have no clear pattern, yet worsen with stress and concentration. That concerns me, Mr. President. It could be simple tension, or it could indicate strain on the brain itself. Until we know more, every hour of overwork is a risk.

Can you — will you — commit to these specific measures? Not as pleasant ideas, but as medical orders?

Thank you, Doctor, for your guidance and for holding me accountable in this matter. Your expertise and care are truly appreciated.

transcript.speaker: antagonist

*relaxes slightly, a hint of cautious satisfaction crossing his face*

I'll return in one week's time to continue my examination. I want to assess your reflexes more thoroughly, examine your eyes under better light, and perhaps perform some additional tests.

Mr. President, may I ask you something more personal? How do you bear it — the weight of so many lives depending on your decisions? I ask not from idle curiosity, but because the mind and body are not separate. Your mental burden affects your physical health profoundly. Do you have... outlets? Ways to process the strain beyond simply working through it?

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*listens intently, then nods with a mixture of approval and lingering concern*

Reading and writing, family, the sustaining power of purpose — these are good things, Mr. President. Better than whiskey and isolation, which is how many men in your position manage their burdens. Still...

*hesitates, choosing his words carefully*

I wonder if even these outlets are sufficient for what you carry. You speak of solitude for reflection, yet solitude can also become rumination — the mind circling endlessly around problems that have no perfect solution. Every decision you make, lives hang in the balance either way. That is not a burden that reading alone can lift.

*leans back in his chair*

Forgive me if I overstep, but have you someone with whom you can speak candidly? Not advisors seeking your decision, not family members you wish to protect from your darker thoughts, but someone who can simply... listen? The confession of uncertainty, of doubt, of grief — these too are necessary for health.

*meets his eyes directly*

I've seen strong men destroy themselves from the inside because they believed they must bear everything alone. You are not Atlas, Mr. President, though the nation sometimes treats you as such.

*pauses*

But perhaps I've wandered too far from my medical duties into philosophy. Still, the question stands — do you have that outlet? Or do you keep your deepest struggles locked away?

transcript.text:
*observes Lincoln quietly for a moment, noting the eloquence of his response and the careful way he navigates even this personal inquiry*

Mr. President, you have a remarkable gift for words — but I notice you have answered my question without quite answering it. You speak of recognizing the necessity, of reflecting on my words, of considering how best to cultivate such an outlet. These are the words of a man who does not yet have what I'm describing.

*stands slowly, collecting his medical bag*

I am a physician, not a priest or a philosopher, so I will not press further. But I will say this: the body keeps score of what the heart holds in. Your headaches, your fatigue — they may be warning signals that you are indeed trying to be Atlas, whether you intend to or not.

*moves toward the door, then pauses*

In one week, I will return to examine you further. Between now and then, I ask you to do something beyond taking the tonic and keeping reasonable hours. I ask you to find one person — perhaps your wife, perhaps an old friend, perhaps even a minister — and speak to them with complete honesty about one burden you carry. Not a policy question. Not a strategic dilemma. But something that weighs on your soul.

*looks back at him with unmistakable concern*

Consider it a medical prescription, Mr. President. The body cannot heal if the spirit remains wounded.

Will you at least try?

*pauses at the door, hand on the handle, and turns back with a small, somewhat weary smile*

Mr. President, I notice you said you will "make an effort" and "consider earnestly." These are still careful, measured words. But I suppose that is all any physician can ask — that his patient will try.

You agree to what is reasonable, you acknowledge what is wise, but I wonder if you truly believe you will follow through, or if circumstances will simply... override your intentions.

Forgive an old doctor his frankness, but I fear for you, sir. Not just your headaches or your fatigue, but something deeper. There is a quality of resignation in you — a sense that you have already accepted whatever cost this office will exact from you.

*softens his tone*

One week, Mr. President. I will see you then. And I genuinely hope when I return, you can tell me you have spoken to someone — truly spoken — about what burdens you most.

*opens the door, then adds quietly*

The nation needs you alive and whole, sir. Not a martyr.

Good day, Mr. President.

*stops in the doorway, back still turned, and stands silent for a long moment*

*finally turns back, his expression more gentle than before*

Mr. President... Abraham, if I may be so bold for just this moment — you have thanked me four times in this conversation. You have acknowledged my wisdom, praised my dedication, and promised to meet my expectations. 

*takes a few steps back into the room*

But I don't want your gratitude or your promises to meet expectations. I want you to *survive* this. Not just physically, but as a man with a soul that still feels, still hopes, still connects to something beyond duty and sacrifice.

*his voice drops, almost gentle*

When I return next week, I don't need a report of your compliance. I need to see in your eyes that you have allowed yourself to be human — if only for an hour. To be not the President, not the savior of the Union, but simply a man who hurts and fears and doubts, speaking to another human being who cares for him.

*picks up his hat from the side table*

That is what I truly prescribe, sir. Not management of my concerns, but genuine unburdening of your own.

*nods once, firmly*

Until next week, then. And may God grant you the courage to be weak with someone who can bear it with you.

*exits quietly, closing the door behind him*
